chapter: On the road with Victor Spencer
title: Jailed in Arkansas and a wedding feud at Church Point
summary: One long story of a feud wedding and being jailed until he taught a sheriff's girl ukulele.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: And Buster Millier was a guy that looked like Gilbert Young, but he played like Sun Johnson. And his daddy used to be the pool walker at the Crowley Social Hall, and he'd come around there that night and all we could do was tell us not to go there. You see we used to go there and get liquor, you know, that used to handle that sheriffs and things, they used to handle all that bad liquor. You understand? And we left there and a couple of days after that we had a date in Church Point. We played a wedding out there, a white wedding, and it was reminding you of the cowboy days. We had to stay a bond about three days. It was a feudal between two families, one didn't want the other to marry the other, and it was like on the right we were all out that way. And we left there and we went on to El Lerato, Arkansas. And we left El Lerato and we went to McGee, Arkansas, we was crossing the street still. The red lights was down in the ground and we crossed the street. And the crankcase, I was with Victor Spencer then, we crossed the crankcase and tore the muffler or something under the car there, oil was leaking. So they put the whole band in jail, you understand? And so they put the whole band in jail there after we got there. And the sheriff said, with a big old ten gallon hat, say, I want you to teach this little girl how to play that fiddle. She had a ukulele. You understand? So I said, well she needs some books to learn how to play that instrument. I said, wait till the music store will open up tomorrow, we'll go down to town and see if I can. So I went down there and got some little books, you know where you put your finger on the ukulele, ain't going to rain no more, ain't going to rain no more, you understand? So the man said, you got to teach you how to play. So Gordy said, how? He said, that's what you get for being a band in jail prayer. Now they going to keep you here. No, now you going to stay here. I said, damn, that's all right, I ain't going to stay here soon. I said, oh yeah, you'll be here a long time until that little girl learned how to play that fiddle. So they kept us there, three or four days, and Judge Farnas said, how much y'all charge to play a dance? A hundred and seventy-five dollars. I said, that's what we're going to find in the audience. A hundred and seventy-five dollars. So we've been just laughing at me. So the little girl's mother said, well, they seem to be a nice bunch of guys. So they gave me twenty dollars for teaching the little girl. So they wanted something. I said, oh no, I was the guy that was going to stay here. You don't get a horn in on this.
